1. 
Report 
on 
The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 
I. Background and Introduction 
Wetlands are vital parts of the hydrological cycle and are highly 
productive ecosystems which support rich biodiversity and provide a wide range 
of ecosystem services. Environmentalists, biologists and others concerned about 
the health of the planet and its inhabitants recognize the key role wetlands play 
in life on Earth.   Wetlands are also key drivers of local economies, given their 
importance to agriculture, recreation and fishing.  However, they are under 
tremendous stress due to rapid urbanization, in dustrialization and agricultural 
intensification, manifested by the shrinkage in their area extent, and decline in 
the hydrological, economic and ecological functions they perform. The pressure 
on wetlands is likely to intensify in the coming decades due t o increased global 
demand for land and water, as well as climate change.  
2. India is one of the 170 Contracting Parties to the Ramsar Convention on 
Wetlands (signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971 and entered into force in 1975), an 
intergovernmental treaty that  provides the framework for n ational action and 
international cooperation for th e conservation and wise use of w etlands and 
their resources. There are 2,477  Ramsar sites across the world. M inistry of 
Environment Forests and Climate Change has so far identified 115 wetlands and 
63 Lakes in 24 States and 2 Union Territories for conservation and management 
under National Wetlands Conservation Program  (NWCP)/National Lake 
Conservation Plan  (NLCP)/National Parks Conservation Association( NPCA). 
The National Envir onment Policy, 2006 recognised the ecosystem services 
provided by wetlands and emphasized on the need to set up a regulatory 
mechanism for all wetlands so as to maintain their ecological character and 
ultimately support their integrated management. (Ref: Preamble to the Wetlands 
Rules, 2017). Thereafter, the Central Government had published the Wetlands 
(Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010, dated the 4th December, 2010. 
However, with the passage of time and experience gained, the Central 
Government considered it necessary to supersede the Wetlands (Conservation 
and Management) Rules, 2010 (hereinafter referred to as 2010 Rules) for 
effective conservation and management of wetlands in the country. Thus in 
exercise of the powers conferred by secti on 25, read with sub -section (1) and 

 
 
2. 
clause (v) of sub -section (2) and sub -section (3) of section 3 and section 23 of 
the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (Annexure I) and in supersession of 
the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010  (Annexure II), the 
Central Government notified the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) 
Rules, 2017 (Annexure III) (hereinafter referred to as 2017 Rules), notified on 
September 26, 2017 for effective conservation and management of wetlands. 
3. The salient features of the Rules are as follows:  
(i) These Rules shall apply to the following wetlands or wetlands complexes, 
namely: (a) wetlands categorised as 'wetlands of international importance' under 
the Ramsar Convention; (b) wetlands as notified by the Central G overnment, 
State Government and Union Territory Administration.  
(ii) The wetlands shall be conserved and managed in accordance with the 
principle of 'wise use' as determined by the Wetlands Authority. 
(iii)The Central Government shall  also constitute the State Wetlands Authority 
in each State. The Central Government shall also constitute the National 
Wetlands Committee which will monitor the implementation of the Rules. The 
authorities, both at the Centre and State level, will have officials from the 
Ministries/Departments  of Environment, Tourism, Water Resources and Rural 
and Urban D evelopment, Fisheries, Revenue , Flood Control   as well as 
members of the Pollution Control Boards among others. 
(iv) The authorities at the State or Union T erritory level have been tasked with 
listing all wetlands in their territories within three months and prepare a list of 
wetlands to be notified, within six months, among other functions, including 
developing a comprehensive list of activities to be regulated and permitted 
within the notified wetlands and their zone of influence. 
II. Examination of Rules, Observations and Recommendations  
 
4. Keeping in view the significance of these Rules in conservation and 
management of wetlands in the country, these  were taken up for detailed 
examination by the Committee.  A detailed questionnaire on the subject was 
forwarded to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for their 
comments/clarifications on 27 th June, 2018. The Ministry furnished their 
comments/clarifications on the 29th June, 2018 (Annexure IV). The Committee 
considered the matter at its meeting held on the 3 rd July, 2018 with the 
Secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change along with 

 
 
3. 
other senior Officials from the Mini stry.  A brief summary of the points raised 
by the Committee and the comments of the Ministry are elaborated in the 
succeeding paragraphs along with the observations/recommendations of the 
Committee.  
5. The Committee enquired about the reasons that led th e Central 
Government to frame the, 2017 Rules and supersede the  2010 Rules. The 
Ministry informed that the Rules have been formulated after taking into 
consideration the problems faced during implementation of the 2010 Rules and 
for a better identification, management and preservation of wetlands with the 
help of State administration. Based on the experience gained from the 
implementation of the 2010 Rules and consultation meetings with States etc., it 
was noticed that the 2010 Rules w ere highly centralized and the States and UTs 
could not assume and discharge their requisite responsibilities effectively for 
conservation and management of wetlands under their jurisdiction and control, 
without which it was not possible to implement the 2 010 Rules. Further, the 
Ministry stated that the 2010 Rules were uniform in nature without reference to 
site characteristics and diversities.  Therefore, for a more effective conservation 
and management of wetlands in the Country , the 2017 Rules were notif ied and 
the 2010 Rules were superseded.  
 In the 2010 R ules, the following provisions were specifically mentioned 
where as the 2017 Rules have totally removed such provisions. 
(i) List of activities that can be undertaken with the permission of state 
monitoring committee. 
(ii) Process of identification of wetland. 
(iii) Provision for appeal by the general public against the decision on 
Authority. 
6. The Committee notes the replies furnished by the Ministry and 
observes that the Ministry’s objective of better identificatio n, management 
and preservation of wetlands is laudable. After a detailed scrutiny of the 
Rules, the Committee, though in broad agreement with the objectives of the 
Rules, considered that these Rules are not as comprehensive as they ought 
to be, given the f act that they superseded the 2010 Rules with the objective 
of improving thereon. On a comparison of the 2017 Rules vis-à-vis the 2010 
Rules, the Committee notes that  Rules of 2010 had some  provisions which 
have been done away with in the 2017 Rules. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should try to revisit the 2017 Rules and try to 

 
 
4. 
accommodate/incorporate some provisions of 2010 Rules in the 2017 Rules  
to bring clarity.  
7.  Rule 9 o f the 2010 Rules stated that “any person aggrieved by the 
decision of the Authority may prefer an appeal to the National Green Tribunal 
constituted under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 within a period of 
sixty days from the date of such decision.” This provision does not exist in the 
2017 Rules. The Committee enquired about the reasons for doing away with 
this provision. The Secretary stated that since Rules are framed under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the provision of Appeal to the judic ial 
bodies for any act is implicit under the Rules. Further, the provision of Appeal 
to the NGT is a part of NGT Act and applies to any Rules framed under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, it was opined that the same need not be 
mentioned again in these rules.  
8. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that, even if the provision of Appeal to the judicial bodies for any act is 
implicit under the Rules as stated by the Secretary in his reply, the 
Ministry can explicitly provi de for provisions relating to appeal, more so, 
because there was already a similar provision, explicitly stated in the 2010 
Rules. There is no plausible reason for not menti oning this provision in the 
2017 Rules. 
9. Rule 2(g)  of the (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 defines 
‘Wetlands’ as: “An area of marsh, fen, peatland or water; whether natural or 
artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, 
brackish or salt, including areas of mar ine water the depth of which at low tide 
does not exceed six meters, but does not include river channels, paddy fields, 
human-made water bodies/tanks specifically constructed for drinking water 
purposes and structures specifically constructed for aquacultu re, salt 
production, recreation and irrigation purposes.”  The 2010 Rules included in 
the definition of wetlands all inland waters such as lakes, reservoir, tanks, 
backwaters, lagoon, creeks, estuaries, etc. However, from the above definition   
it is observed that 2017 Rules are not as comprehensive as the old ones. They do 
not include river channels, paddy fields, human -made water bodies/tanks 
specifically for drinking water purposes, aquaculture, salt production, and 
recreation and irrigation purposes. It also does not include wetlands under forest 
and coastal regulation zones. In view thereof t he Committee enquired from the 
Ministry about the justification for adopting this narrow and limited definition 

 
 
5. 
of wetlands in the 2017 Rules. The Ministry informed t hat in the 2017 Rules, 
human-made water bodies/tanks specifically constructed for drinking water 
purposes and structures specifically constructed for aquaculture, salt production, 
recreation & irrigation purposes have been excluded from the definition of 
wetland. It further stated that these Rules shall also not apply to the wetlands 
falling in areas covered under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, the Wild Life 
(Protection) Act, 1972, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the State Forest 
Acts, and the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2011 as amended from time 
to time. The Ministry informed that the justification for the same is that they are 
already protected under other regulations an d this would enable the States and  
UTs to focus on the wetlands having no protection/regulation.  The Secretary 
further stated that human made water bodies are created for the specific 
purposes and if these are regulated under the 2017 Rules , these may not serve 
the purpose they are meant for due to regulation or prohibition of activities 
under the 2017 rules.  
10. The Committee also noted that Salt pans as ‘wetlands’ have been omitted 
from the new Rules. While these were identified as wetlands in the 2010 Rules, 
as they are often important sites for migratory birds and other for ms of wildlife. 
Thus the Ministry was specifically asked about the justification for omission of 
salt pans from the definition of wetlands.  The Secretary stated that salt pans 
were deliberately omitted because these are human made pans and not original 
wetlands.  Upon an enquiry from the Chairman about the reasons for omitting 
lakes, lagoons, creeks, the Secretary stated that backwaters, lagoons, etc., are 
already under the CRZ Rules and that the Ministry is managing them through 
those Rules and that’s why they have not been included.   
11. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that by undoing the protection for India’s already threatened wetlands by 
playing with definitions, the Ministry seems to have increased the 
vulnerability of these hydrologically sensitive area s. The widespread 
expansion of development  in the country in recent decades has only 
contributed towards making these sensitive areas even more vulnerable.  
The Committee feels that if left unchanged, the new Rules might facilitate 
the legal exploitation and development of wetlands as real estate, industrial 
sites and garbage dumps. For a country battling droughts , large scale 
pollution and floods caused by destructive land -use change and climate 
change, the new wetland rules can have disastrous consequences. Under the 
2010 Rules, in addition to Ramsar and government -notified wetlands, any 

 
 
6. 
high-altitude wetland larger than 5 hectares, or those at elevations less than 
2,500 metres and spread over 500 hectares automatically qualified for 
protection. So did wetl ands located in ecologically sensitive areas or areas 
recognised as or lying within UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This 
provision should be reinstated in the 2017 Rules. The Committee is also not 
convinced with the reasons for the omission of salt pans from the definition 
of ‘wetlands’ in the new Rules. Further, since salt pans have been removed, 
even the natural salt pans would fall outside the scope of the new Rules and 
hence are vulnerable to their commercial exploitation. These were 
identified as wetlands in the 2010 Rules, as they are often important sites of 
migratory birds and other forms of biodiversity. Hence, the omission in the 
2017 Rules implies that while salt  pans do exist as wetlands, they do not 
require any conservation or ecological balance.  
12. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the natural salt pans 
should be given protection under the Rules , given their significance as 
important sites for migratory birds and other forms of biodiversity. The 
Committee further notes that in the 2010 Ru les, some related criteria for 
identification of wetlands , which require protection  were made explicit, 
such as natural beauty, ecological sensitivity, genetic diversity, historical 
value, etc. However, these have been omitted in the 2017 Rules. This seems  
to be a retrograde step. The Committee notes with concern the definition of 
wetlands in 2017 Rules and recommends that the Ministry should revisit 
the narrow definition of wetlands in 2017 Rules and should include natural 
salt pans in the definition and emphasis should be given on protection of 
wetlands that protect wildlife and biodiversity.  The Committee further 
recommends that the criteria for identification of wetlands requiring 
protection which were explicitly mentioned in the 2010 Rules may be r e-
introduced in the present Ru les so that a clear cut  basis for selecting salt 
pan from the point of view of wildlife and biodiversity could be made out 
from the legislation itself rather than completely removing the  same from 
Rules.  Further, given the immen se significance of wetlands in 
environmental conservation, an action taken Note may be  expeditiously 
provided to the Committee.  The Committee also observed that in many 
places paddy fields are lying idle for many years due to various reasons and 
they are s erving the purpose of water storage, floo d mitigation, acquifer 
recharge etc. so such idle paddy fields etc for  a longer period of 10 years or 
more may be brought under these rules. The classification of such paddy 

 
 
7. 
fields may be done and records  be updated as the cases may be.  Similarly 
the Silica mining/granite mining sites and quarie s have good water holding 
capacity which is also to be included  in the wetland category and required  
to be conserved.  
13. Rule 7 provides for  “Delegation of powers and functions to the State 
Governments and Union Territory Administrations.”  This Rule, which is newly 
introduced, puts the onus on the S tate governments to prepare brie f documents 
on each wetland identified for notification containing demarcation of the 
boundary, list out activities that would be permitted or regulated within the 
wetland or its zone of influence and also to work out modalities for enforcement 
of the Regulation. The State or Union Territory wetland authorities would make 
recommendations based on this document for notifying the wetlands. And in 
case of trans -boundary wetlands, the central Government will co -ordinate with 
concerned States/UTs for the above activity. The Ministry was asked to respond 
to the criticism that the 2017 Rules source out  wetland management to States 
and Union Territories despite there being lethargic responses from States and 
Union Territories in the past on wetland protection. The Committee feels that 
devolving management to States and Union Territories in their totality  could 
make wetland conservation ineffective. The Ministry stated in a written reply to 
the Committee that Central Government is conscious  of its obligations to 
protect environment, however, the subjects of Water and Land fall within the 
State List under E ntry 18 of list 2 of schedule 7 of the Constitution of India. 
Therefore, constitutionally, it is the State Governments which have to execute 
the same. The Ministry further stated that the Environment (Protection) Act, 
1986, as well as Article 253 read with  Entry 13 and 14 of Seventh Schedule is 
in terms of the law making power of the Parliament. Hence, law is made by the 
Parliament and Rules are made by the Central Government but actual 
implementation has to be done by State Governments. The Ministry furthe r 
stated that the power to implement and execute particular provision has always 
been delegated to the State Government, under the Constitution itself with 
federal structure and states as federating units. The Ministry also informed that 
State Governments have adequate machinery and departments to deal with the 
information pertaining to land and water bodies. Therefore, the State 
Governments are in a better posit ion to identify and notify the w etlands. The 
Ministry informed the Committee that an empowered authority consisting of the 
officers of the State Government has been created to facilitate time bound 
identification of wetlands which is otherwise also a State subject. The creation 

 
 
8. 
of State and UT Wetlands Authorities is intended to facilitate the time bound 
identification of wetlands and it does not detract from the powers vested with 
the Central Government to issue appropriate orders and directions for fulfilment 
of the objective of the 2017 Rules.  
14. The Secretary further informed the Committee that the 2010 Rules 
needed certain amendments which were based on the knowledge that was 
gained while implementation of 2010 Rules. The  Secretary stated that the 2010 
Rules had become completely c entred and concentrated in the Union 
Government and the States had very little role.  As a result, when things were 
decided at Central level, the implementation was very difficult at the field level.  
So, it was decided that it is better that the Ministry focuses on implementation.  
To improve implementation, 2017 Rules were introduced, wherein the biggest 
attempt that was made was at decentralising powers to the State Gover nments 
and the Wetland Authorities there, so that they can take care of what they wa nt 
to do.  The Secretary further observed that when there is a much centralised 
system, it is a common prescription for all wetlands across the country, and 
wetlands differ both in size and site  and they need separate treatments.  That 
was another reason why this decentralisation was done by the Ministry.   
15.  The Committee is not convinced with the clarification of the Ministry that 
land and water fall in the State List and hence the wetlands management should 
also fall within the purview of the State/UT  Governments. The committee feels 
that Forest and Protection of Wild Animals and Birds, which comes at entry 
17A and 17B of the Concurrent List is the relevant provision for the present 
case. Further, the Committee  appreciates the efforts of the  Ministry t o 
decentralise the implementation of these Regulations, However, it cannot 
simply wash it hands off from the huge responsibility on it to protect, conserve 
and improve the quality of wildlife and forest gifted by mother earth to us, 
which is deteriorating every day. 
16. The Committee observes that new rules have done away with the 
National Wetlands Authority created under the 2010 R ules and conferred 
all regulatory powers on the State governments. The Centre’s act of 
abdicating its responsibilities is claim ed to be a virtuous move to 
decentralise in the spirit of federalism.  However, environmentalists say 
this is odd, as States and UTs have never acted on wetlands protection and 
notification in spite of the pressure exerted by the Central government — 
using the Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority (CWRA) — under the 

 
 
9. 
2010 Rules. The Committee expects the Ministry to play a pro-active role in 
the implementation of the Rules and recommends that the implementation 
of the Rules must be a joint responsibility of the Centre and the States. The 
Centre should not abdicate its constitutional responsibility and obligation 
to protect the wetlands and the environment. The Committee also 
recommends that the Central Government should extend any kind of 
feasible help, be it  in terms of manpower, infrastructure or financial aid, 
which may be needed by the States to preserve and protect the wetlands 
within their territory. 
17. Under the Rule 5(4)(n), the State wetland authorities can issue necessary 
directions for conservation  and sustainable management of wetlands to the 
respective implementing agencies. However, the directions are not binding in 
nature to desist from any activity detrimental to wetland conservation. The 
Ministry was asked to explain the reasons for the directions not being backed by 
a penal sanction.  The Ministry in a written reply to the Committee stated that 
penal provision can be made only in an Act of Parliament and not in the 
subordinate legislation. The Ministry further informed that it is in the process of 
amending the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 w.r.t civil penalties. 
However, the Secretary informed the Committee that there is a lack of enough 
awareness in this country on conservation and preservation of these wetlands.  
He stated that any amount  of legal framework that is created will not succeed 
unless that kind of awareness is generated at local level because wetlands are 
used by people every day.   
18. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that since penal provision  can be made only in an Act of Parliament and 
not in the subordinate legislation, therefore, the Ministry should expedite 
the process of amending the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to provide 
for civil penalties, if the directions issued by the State w etland authorities 
to the respective implementing agencies for conservation and sustainable 
management of wetlands are not adhered to. The amendment should 
clearly provide for the institutional mechanism to pursue cases of non 
compliance with the direction s issued by the State wetland authorities and 
the penalty should be sufficient enough to act as a deterrent. 
19. Rule 6 provides for constitution of National Wetlands Committee. The 
Committee noted that the 2017 Rules have done away with the Central 
Wetlands Regulatory Authority (CWRA) that was provided under the 2010 

 
 
10. 
Rules. CWRA’s place has been taken by the National Wetlands Committee, 
which has a merely advisory role. The Committee enquired about the reasons 
and necessity for such a step.  The Ministry st ated that it was envisaged that 
decentralization of functions and responsibilities can yield better results in the 
matter of preservation of land or water bodies. It informed the Committee that 
the National Wetlands Committee (NWC)  is constituted under the  2017 Rules 
and is categorically entrusted with the job to monitor implementation of the 
rules by the State and Union Territory (UT) Wetlands Authorities in addition to 
its advisory role. The Ministry further informed that NWC shall advise Central 
Government on appropriate policies and action programmes for conservation 
and wise use of wetlands, monitor implementation of the Wetlands Rules by 
concerned Wetlands Authorities, recommend new Ramsar Sites, recommend 
trans-boundary wetlands for notification under  these rules, review progress of 
integrated management of Ramsar sites and transboundary wetlands etc.  
20. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that the Ministry has not offered sufficient justification or rationale for 
doing away with the Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority (CWRA) that 
was provided under the 2010 Rules and replacing it with the National 
Wetlands Committee, which has a merely advisory role.  However, if the 
Ministry still feels compelled to continue with the National Wetlands 
Committee, then it should be given enough ‘teeth’ to enforce its directions 
and pursue its recommendations. It should not be a ‘toothless’ body and 
should be sufficiently empowered to enforce its mandate.  
21. Rule 4 (Restrictions of activities in wetlands), says that conservation and 
management of wetlands would be “in accordance with the principle of „wise 
use‟ as determined by the Wetlands Authority”.  The Committee noted that 
environmentalists have criticized this principle. Their conce rn is that how does 
one define ‘wise use’? It’s a very subjective term. The Ministry was asked about 
its views on this issue?  The Ministry stated that ‘Wise use’ has been defined as 
maintenance of their ecological character, achieved through implementation  of 
ecosystem approach within the context of sustainable development in the rules 
and is an accepted principle globally including the ‘Ramsar Convention’ on 
wetlands, an intergovernmental treaty which provides framework for national 
action for conservation  of wetlands. The Secretary further stated that the 
Ministry has initiated the process for formulation of Guidelines for 2017 Rules 
which shall inter-alia, guide on the technical terms such as ecological character, 

 
 
11. 
integrated management plan, wetlands complexes, wise use of wetlands, zone of 
influence used in the Rules.  
22. The Committee notes with concern that restriction of activities on 
wetlands will be done as per the principle of ‘wise use’, determined by the 
State Wetlands Authority. The Committee recommends that the term ‘wise 
use’ must be defined or clear parameters must be laid down to identify 
‘wise use’ so that there is no space for ambiguity or multiple 
interpretations of this term. The Committee also directs that the process 
for formulation of Guidelines for 2017 Rules which shall inter -alia, guide 
on the technical terms shall be completed as soon as possible and those 
guidelines should also be furnished to the Committee for its perusal. 
23. Rule 5(6) makes provisions for a Grievance Committee t o be constituted 
by the State Wetlands Authority, to provide a mechanism for hearing and 
forwarding the grievances raised by public to the Authority. However, the Rules 
do not provide for an appeal there from.  The Ministry was asked about the 
reasons for not providing a forum to make appeals against the decision of the 
Authority. The Ministry stated that since the provision of Appeal to the Hon’ble 
NGT is a part of NGT Act and applies to any Rules framed under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, it was  opined that the same need not be 
mentioned again in 2017 rules.  
24. The Committee observes from the replies fu rnished by the Ministry 
that  since the provision of Appeal to the Hon’ble NGT is applicable to the 
present Rules, therefore it would bring only  more transparency if it is 
made explicit in the Rules that appeal to NGT can be made against a 
decision of State Wetlands Authority.  
25. Under Rule 6(xviii),  one expert each in the fields of wetland ecology, 
hydrology, fisheries, landscape planning and socio -economic planning is to be 
appointed as a member of the National Wetlands Committee. The Committee 
enquired about the criterion for appointing such members and whether there any 
minimum eligibility qualifications prescribed for being appointed as a member 
of the Committee. The Ministry replied that no minimum eligibility 
qualifications have been prescribed. However, experts are always appointed 
based on their qualifications and work experience. 
26. The Committee strongly feels  that certain minimum 
eligibility/qualifications shall be prescribed for being appointed as a 

 
 
12. 
member of the National Wetlands Committee so that no arbitrary 
appointments are made to the  Committee and members are appointed on 
merit and not on any extraneous considerations or political affiliations. 
27. Further the Committee believes that Gram Panchayats are the bodies 
controlling land use in a  particular area, in each State . So the 
representation of the Panchayat authorities also need to be ensured in the 
Committee 
28. Rule 4 lists a range of prohibited activities within notified wetlands. But 
a proviso to it allows the Centre to omit any activities from this list if the State 
Wetlands Aut hority recommends it. A common criticism of t he Rules is that 
whatever minute  protection is offered is also discretionary. The Committee 
enquired the views of the Ministry on the need and justification for this proviso.   
The Ministry stated that the decision making power for any deviations from the 
prohibited activities within the wetland is vested with the Central Government 
in both the 2010 and 2017 Rules. In fact, such proposals recommended by t he 
State and UT Wetlands Authorities shall in turn be placed before the National 
Wetlands Committee for its recommendation as per Rule 6(3)(d) of the 2017 
Rules. The Ministry informed the Committee that the need for this proviso is 
upon consideration of the diversity in issues across the vast country. 
29. The Committee notes with concern that this proviso to omit activities 
from the list of prohibited activities in the state committee recommendation          
gives ample space to the Authorities to permit activities which ought to be 
prohibited. The proviso als o lends credence to the criticism of the Rules 
that whatever little protection is offered is also discretionary. The 
Committee accordingly recommends that this proviso should ideally not be 
there in Rules but if the Ministry still believes that its essenti al, then a 
check and balance may be added to ensure that the proviso is not misused 
to diminish the protection given to wetlands under the Rules.  For instance, 
a requirement may be added that if the Centre omits any activities from 
the list of notified we tlands then that omission should be approved by the 
NGT or some independent committee set up for the purpose, in a time 
bound manner. 
30. The Committee enquired that whether the R ules are enough to take care 
of all the illegal activities in wetlands and coastal areas and if they are 
sufficient, then why do these illegal activities still happen. The Secretary stated 
that they are absolutely sufficient and added that in fact, the Min istry is accused 

 
 
13. 
of having one of the toughest coastal zone regulations in the world. However, 
he admitted that the provisions are not effectively implemented and the Ministry 
is working on how to make the implementation of Rules more effective.  
31. The C ommittee notes with concern the tardy implementation of 
Rules and  observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry that steps 
should be taken to make the implementation of Rules more effective. The 
Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that proper monitoring 
and inspection are essential for the proper and effective implementation of 
Rules and Regulations, and stresses upon the Ministry to strengthen its 
enforcement mechanism to ensure that the objectives of the Rules are 
achieved. If required , the Ministry should come out with necessary 
amendments in the Rules or the Environment Protection Act, 1986 to 
secure effective compliance with the provisions of these Rules. A 
Committee may also be constituted within the Ministry, headed by a senior 
bureaucrat or a noted environmentalist/renowned academician to monitor 
the implementation of these Rules and report or make recommendations 
about problems faced in implementation, if any. The Ministry can also 
provide for a informants reward  scheme for concer ned and proactive  
citizens to report illegal activities such as filling, clearing, or dumping in 
wetlands to government authorities. 
32. The Committee is hopeful that the Ministry would carry out the 
recommendations of the Committee expeditiously under intimation to it.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
14. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE - AT 
A GLANCE 
1. The Committee notes the replies furnished by the Ministry and 
observes that the Ministry’s objective of better identification, management 
and preservation of wetlands is laudable. After a detailed scrutiny of the 
Rules, the Committee, though in broad agreement with the objectives of the 
Rules, considered that these Rules are not as comprehensive as they ought 
to be, given the fact that they superseded the 2010 Rules with the objective 
of improving thereon. On a comparison of the 2017 Rules vis-à-vis the 2010 
Rules, the Committee notes that Rules of 2010 had some provisions which 
have been done away with in the 2017 Rules. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should try to revisit the 2017 Rules and try to 
accommodate/incorporate some provisions of 2010 Ru les in the 2017 Rules 
to bring clarity.  
(Para 6) 
 
2. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that, even if the provision of Appeal to the judicial bodies for any act is 
implicit under the Rules as stated by the Secretary in his r eply, the 
Ministry can explicitly provide for provisions relating to appeal, more so, 
because there was already a similar provision, explicitly stated in the 2010 
Rules. There is no plausible reason for not mentioning this provision in the 
2017 Rules. 
(Para 8) 
 
3. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that by undoing the protection for India’s already threatened wetlands by 
playing with definitions, the Ministry seems to have increased the 
vulnerability of these hydrologically se nsitive areas. The widespread 
expansion of development  in the country in recent decades has only 
contributed towards making these sensitive areas even more vulnerable.  
The Committee feels that if left unchanged, the new Rules might facilitate 
the legal exploitation and development of wetlands as real estate, industrial 
sites and garbage dumps. For a country battling droughts, large scale 
pollution and floods caused by destructive land -use change and climate 
change, the new wetland rules can have disastrous consequences. Under the 
2010 Rules, in addition to Ramsar and government -notified wetlands, any 

 
 
15. 
high-altitude wetland larger than 5 hectares, or those at elevations less than 
2,500 metres and spread over 500 hectares automatically qualified for 
protection. So did wetlands located in ecologically sensitive areas or areas 
recognised as or lying within UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This 
provision should be reinstated in the 2017 Rules. The Committee is also not 
convinced with the reasons for the omission of sal t pans from the definition 
of ‘wetlands’ in the new Rules. Further, since salt pans have been removed, 
even the natural salt pans would fall outside the scope of the new Rules and 
hence are vulnerable to their commercial exploitation. These were 
identified as wetlands in the 2010 Rules, as they are often important sites of 
migratory birds and other forms of biodiversity. Hence, the omission in the 
2017 Rules implies that while salt pans do exist as wetlands, they do not 
require any conservation or ecological balance.  
(Para 11) 
 
4. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the natural salt pans should 
be given protection under the Rules, given their significance as important 
sites for migratory birds and other forms of biodiversity. The Committee 
further notes that in the 2010 Rules, some related criteria for identification 
of wetlands, which require protection were made explicit, such as natural 
beauty, ecological sensitivity, genetic diversity, historical value, etc. 
However, these have been omitted in the 2017 Rules. This seems to be a 
retrograde step. The Committee notes with concern the definition of 
wetlands in 2017 Rules and recommends that the Ministry should revisit 
the narrow definition of wetlands in 2017 Rules and should include natural 
salt pans i n the definition and emphasis should be given on protection of 
wetlands that protect wildlife and biodiversity. The Committee further 
recommends that the criteria for identification of wetlands requiring 
protection which were explicitly mentioned in the 20 10 Rules may be re -
introduced in the present Rules so that a clear cut  basis for selecting salt 
pan from the point of view of wildlife and biodiversity could be made out 
from the legislation itself rather than completely removing the same from 
Rules.  Fur ther, given the immense significance of wetlands in 
environmental conservation, an action taken Note may be expeditiously 
provided to the Committee. The Committee also observed that in many 
places paddy fields are lying idle for many years due to various reasons and 
they are serving the purpose of water storage, flood mitigation, acquifer 
recharge etc. so such idle paddy fields etc for a longer period of 10 years or 

 
 
16. 
more may be brought under these rules. The classification of such paddy 
fields may be done a nd records be updated as the cases may be.  Similarly 
the Silica mining/granite mining sites and quaries have good water holding 
capacity which is also to be included in the wetland category and required 
to be conserved.  
(Para 12) 
 
5. The Committee observ es that new rules have done away with the 
National Wetlands Authority created under the 2010 Rules and conferred 
all regulatory powers on the State governments. The Centre’s act of 
abdicating its responsibilities is claimed to be a virtuous move to 
decentralise in the spirit of federalism.  However, environmentalists say 
this is odd, as States and UTs have never acted on wetlands protection and 
notification in spite of the pressure exerted by the Central government — 
using the Central Wetlands Regulatory Au thority (CWRA) — under the 
2010 Rules. The Committee expects the Ministry to play a pro-active role in 
the implementation of the Rules and recommends that the implementation 
of the Rules must be a joint responsibility of the Centre and the States. The 
Centre should not abdicate its constitutional responsibility and obligation 
to protect the wetlands and the environment. The Committee also 
recommends that the Central Government should extend any kind of 
feasible help, be it in terms of manpower, infrastructu re or financial aid, 
which may be needed by the States to preserve and protect the wetlands 
within their territory. 
(Para 16) 
 
6. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that since penal provision can be made only in an Act of Parliament and 
not in the subordinate legislation, therefore, the Ministry should expedite 
the process of amending the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to provide 
for civil penalties, if the directions issued by the State wetland authorities 
to the respe ctive implementing agencies for conservation and sustainable 
management of wetlands are not adhered to. The amendment should 
clearly provide for the institutional mechanism to pursue cases of non 
compliance with the directions issued by the State wetland a uthorities and 
the penalty should be sufficient enough to act as a deterrent. 
(Para 18) 
 

 
 
17. 
7. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that the Ministry has not offered sufficient justification or rationale for 
doing away with the Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority (CWRA) that 
was provided under the 2010 Rules and replac ing it with the National 
Wetlands Committee, which has a merely advisory role.  However, if the 
Ministry still feels compelled to continue with the National Wetlands 
Committee, then it should be given enough ‘teeth’ to enforce its directions 
and pursue its  recommendations. It should not be a ‘toothless’ body and 
should be sufficiently empowered to enforce its mandate.  
(Para 20) 
 
8. The Committee notes with concern that restriction of activities on 
wetlands will be done as per the principle of ‘wise use’, d etermined by the 
State Wetlands Authority. The Committee recommends that the term ‘wise 
use’ must be defined or clear parameters must be laid down to identify 
‘wise use’ so that there is no space for ambiguity or multiple 
interpretations of this term. The Committee also directs that the process 
for formulation of Guidelines for 2017 Rules which shall inter -alia, guide 
on the technical terms shall be completed as soon as possible and those 
guidelines should also be furnished to the Committee for its perusal. 
(Para 22) 
 
9. The Committee observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry 
that  since the provision of Appeal to the Hon’ble NGT is applicable to the 
present Rules, therefore it would bring only more transparency if it is 
made explicit in the Rules that appeal to NGT can be made against a 
decision of State Wetlands Authority.  
(Para 24) 
 
10. The Committee strongly feels that certain minimum 
eligibility/qualifications shall be prescribed for being appointed as a 
member of the National Wetlands Committ ee so that no arbitrary 
appointments are made to the Committee and members are appointed on 
merit and not on any extraneous considerations or political affiliations. 
(Para 26) 
 
11. Further the Committee believes that Gram Panchayats are the bodies 
controlling land use in a particular area, in each State. So the 

 
 
18. 
representation of the Panchayat authorities also need to be ensured in the 
Committee 
(Para 27) 
 
12. The Committee notes with concern that this proviso to omit activities 
from the list of prohibited activities in the state committee recommendation 
gives ample space to the Authorities to permit activities which ought to be 
prohibited. The proviso also lends credence to the criticism of the Rules 
that whatever little protection is offered is also discret ionary. The 
Committee accordingly recommends that this proviso should ideally not be 
there in Rules but if the Ministry still believes that its essential, then a 
check and balance may be added to ensure that the proviso is not misused 
to diminish the protection given to wetlands under the Rules.  For instance, 
a requirement may be added that if the Centre omits any activities from 
the list of notified wetlands then that omission should be approved by the 
NGT or some independent committee set up for the purp ose, in a time 
bound manner. 
(Para 29) 
 
13. The Committee notes with concern the tardy implementation of 
Rules and  observes from the replies furnished by the Ministry that steps 
should be taken to make the implementation of Rules more effective. The 
Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that proper monitoring 
and inspection are essential for the proper and effective implementation of 
Rules and Regulations, and stresses upon the Ministry to strengthen its 
enforcement mechanism to ensure that the objectives of the Rules are 
achieved. If required, the Ministry should come out with necessary 
amendments in the Rules or the Environment Protection Act, 1986 to 
secure effective compliance with the provisions of these Rules. A 
Committee may also be constituted within the Ministry, headed by a senior 
bureaucrat or a noted environmentalist/renowned academician to monitor 
the implementation of these Rules and report or make recommendations 
about problems faced in implementation, if any. The Ministry can also 
provide for a informants reward scheme for concerned and proactive 
citizens to report illegal activities such as filling, clearing, or dumping in 
wetlands to government authorities. 
(Para 31) 

 
 
19. 
14. The Committee is hopeful that the Ministry would carry out t he 
recommendations of the Committee expeditiously under intimation to it.  
(Para 32)

5.  Thereafter, the Committee took up for discussion the Wetlands (Conservation and 
Management) Rules, 2017 with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change . 
The Committee enquired from the Secretary about the objectives sought to be achieved by 
framing the Rules and the salient features of the Rules.  The Secretary informed the 
Committee that the Rules of 2010 needed certain amendments which were based on the 
knowledge that was gained while implementing them.  He stated that the Rules of 2010 had 
become completely centred and concentrated in the Union Government and the States had 
very little role.  As a result, when things were decided at Union Ministry level, the 
implementation was very difficult at the field level.  So, the Ministry decided that it is better 
that it focuses on implementation and decentralise powers to the State Governments and the 
Wetland Authority there. On an enquiry about the justification for adopting a narrow and 
limited definition of Wetlands in the 2017 Rules compared to th e wider definition in 2010 
Rules, the Secretary informed the Committee that the 2017 Rules did not include things like 
river channels, paddy fields, water bodies, water  for drinking purposes, or salt production 
purposes as all these are human made systems and are not original wetland systems.  He 
further stated that whatever was covered by the Forests Act or CRZ Regulation was also not 
taken in the Wetland Rules of 2017.   The Committee enquired from the Ministry whether the 
rules are enough to take care of  all the illegal activities in wetlands and coastal areas. The

accused of having one of the toughest coastal zonal regulations in the world. However , he

INTRODUCTION 
1.  I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been 
authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Two Hundred and 
Fifty Third Report of the Committee. 
2. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha is constituted under 
Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. 
The mandate of the Committee is to scrutinize  and report to Rajya Sabha  whether the 
powers to make  Rules, Regulations, Bye -laws, Schemes and other statutory 
instruments conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament have been 
properly exercised within such conferment or delegation as the case may be. 
3. The Rules/Regulations/Orders etc. are required to be framed within six months 
of the coming into force of the particular Act.  However, the Committee noticed that 
despite the time limit prescribed for completion of framing of subordinate legislation 
and the several ob servations and recommendations of the Committee on the matter, 
various Acts are still pending since many years in various Ministries.   
4. The Committee's apprehension is also focused around the serious implications 
of delay in making of Rules and Regulati ons. Therefore, the Ministries under whom 
Acts are pending for a considerable time were identified and heard in two spells on 
29th May and 30 th June, 2023 in the meetings held with the Ministries to know the 
reasons for delay and the problems faced by the Ministries in framing the 
rules/regulations, etc. This report is prepared on the basis of these deliberations and its 
observations/recommendations are contained in the Report.  
5. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report in its meeting held on  
5th October, 2023.

REPORT  
Committee on Subordinate Legislation and its roles 
1. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha has been set up to scrutinize 
and report to the House whether the powers to make rules, regulations, bye -laws, schemes or 
other statutory instruments conferred by the Constitution or delegated by the Parliament have 
been properly exercised within such conferment or delegation, as the case may be. 
Functions of the Committee: 
2. Rule 209 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha lays 
down the functions of the Committee thus: 
 After each rule, regulation, bye -law, scheme or other statut ory instrument (hereinafter 
referred to as the ‘order’) framed in pursuance of the Constitution or the legislative functions 
delegated by Parliament to a subordinate authority and which is required to be laid before 
Parliament, is so laid before the Council, the Committee shall, in particular consider 
 i. Whether the order is in accord with the provisions of the Constitution or the Act 
 pursuant to which it is made; 
 ii. Whether the order contains matter which in the opinion of the Committee should   
 more properly be dealt within an Act of Parliament; 
 iii. Whether the order contains imposition of taxation; 
 iv. Whether the order directly or indirectly bars the jurisdiction of the court; 
 v. Whether the order gives retrospective effect to any of the provisi ons in respect of                  
which    the Constitution or the Act does not expressly give any such power; 
 vi. Whether the order involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India or the 
 public revenues; 
 vii. Whether the order appears to make some unusual or unexpected use of the powers 
 conferred by the Constitution or the Act pursuant to which it is made; 
viii. Whether there appears to have been unjustifiable delay in its publication or laying      
the order before Parliament; and 
 ix. Whether for any reason the form or purport of the order calls for any elucidation.
  

 
 
 
2 
 
3. Besides the functions as enumerated in Rule 209, the Committee goes into matters, 
where the rules, regulations, bye -laws and other statutory instruments as contemplated in th e 
Constitution or envisaged in an Act of Parliament have not been framed or the framing 
thereof has been inordinately delayed. The Committee also monitors the timely laying of 
notifications containing the subordinate legislations. 
4. The Committee in its Ninth Report has recommended that rules/regulations required to 
be made under a statute should be made as soon as possible and in no case later than six 
months from the date on which the statute comes into force. As a follow up to this, the 
Committee, in it s Forty -seventh Report, recommended that if it was not possible for a 
Ministry to adhere to this time schedule, it should intimate to the Committee the reasons 
therefor and seek extension of time for completing the rule making process. 
5. A Statute can be fully enforced only when all the subordinate legislation s stipulated 
under the Act are framed in time. The Committee, while carrying out its work, has found that 
the Ministries have taken  considerable time in framing  the rules/regulations and , therefore, 
the Acts remain unimplemented or partially implemented.  The Committee  has, however, 
found that most of the Ministries do not adhere to the time limit of six months prescribed by it 
for framing the  rules/regulations. The Committee has noted that delay in framing the  
rules/regulations has become a recurring phenomenon and the matters, which are sought to be 
governed by statutory rules, are often in actual practice governed by executive directions , 
guidelines, etc. in absence of properly framed statutory rul es. This situation often leaves 
scope for corruption and favouritism. 
6. Further, regarding seeking extension of time for framing the  Rules from the 
Committee, the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, has specifically mentioned in Para  11.3.2 
of Manual of Parliamentary Procedures in the Government of India as under:- 
  “In case the departments are not able to frame the rules within the prescribed 
 period of six months, they should seek extension of time from the Committee on 
 Subordinate Legislation stating r easons for such extension; such extension being not 
 more than for a period of three months at a time. The request should be made after 
 obtaining the approval of the Minister.” 
7. The Secretariat, on behalf of the Committee, is regularly sending reminders  to the 
concerned Ministries to speed up the process of framing the rules and regulations which are 
pending with them under the Acts of Parliament.  Besides this, a quarterly statement of the 

 
 
 
3 
 
Acts on which such pendencies lies with the Ministries is forwarded to the Cabinet Secretariat 
for information and further action on its part.   
8. Despite such detailed guidelines and the efforts of the Secretariat; the recommendation 
of the Committee regarding framing the subordinate legislations under a Statute with in six 
months is not being followed by various Ministries. In many of the cases, the Mini stries have 
apologized for the delays and assured strict compliance of the recommendations/observations 
of the Committee in future.  Seeking an extension of time has be come a regular phenomenon, 
whereas framing of subordinate legislation s is being kept in abeyance by some of the 
Ministries.

India on the 10 th September, 2013 and the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public 
Distribution administers  the Act. Central Government is required to frame the Rules under 
Section 39 of the Act and State Governments are required to frame the  Rules under Section 
40 of the Act. During the meeting, the Secretary, Department of Food and Public Distribution 
informed the Committee that all the Rules under Section 39 have been framed and laid on the 
Table of both the Houses of Parliament and nothing was pending on the part of the Central 
Government. He, however, informed that under Section 40, Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand 
were yet to frame the same and their actions were pending as on date. In Delhi four Rules are 
yet to be made operational which may be made operational. The notification of such  Rules in 
Rajasthan is at the final stage and draft rules have been finalized in Uttarakhand. He also 
stated that the Ministry is making regular consultations with the State Governments to 
expedite the action. The Committee noticed that the total delay in framing the subordinate 
legislations under the Act has been more than eight years.

ago, the Rule making process has been stuck up especially on the part of State

or delayed. The Committee also raises concern about the manner in which the  
implementation of the Act in States  is being done  where rules were not framed and also

14.  The Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019 was assented to  by the 
President on the 9th August, 2019 further to amend the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 
Subsequent to the said amendment, Section 43(B)(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 
1996 provides for establishment of a Council to be known as the Arbitration Council of India 
(ACI). Further, various Rules a nd Regulations to be framed under the Act post amendment 
are contemplated under Sections 43 C (3), 43 C (4), 43 M (2), 43 M (4), 43 M (5) and 43 L of 
the Act respectively.  T he Ministry had earlier, while seeking extension(s) of time from the 
Committee for  framing the Subordinate Legislation contemplated under the Act, informed 
that four Rules under Section 43C(3), 43C(4), 43M(2), 43M(4) and 43M (5) respectively had 
been framed, notified and laid on the table of the House on 28.07.2022 . As for the 
Regulations to be framed under the Act, the Ministry had informed that the same would be 
framed by ACI after it is constituted. It was noted by the Committee that even after passing of 
more than 3 years since the Act came into force and granting of extensions five times to the 
Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs), framing of some of the 
Subordinate Legislations under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was still pending.    
15. As regards the reasons for delay, the representatives of Depa rtment informed the 
Committee that a number of stakeholders have demanded autonomy for the ACI and to enable 
establishment of the ACI as an autonomous body, a proposal for comprehensive amendment 
of the Arbitration and Conciliation act, 1996 was under cons ideration in the Department, due 
to which the ACI could not be setup till date . They also mentioned that there was a rethinking 
in the Government that there is a need to work upon revamping the Arbitration Act and bring 
it as a new stand -alone Act because the conciliation aspect of this Act is merged in the 
Mediation Act. Subject to the approval of the Government, the Bill for amending the Act, 
providing for a revamped ACI in its composition and structure, may be introduced in the 
upcoming Session of the Parliament. 
16. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that all the efforts and exercise 
for making sub ordinate legislations under the A ct after its passage  in the year 2019 
might have gone in vain in the circumstances explained by the Department . The ACI, 
which is expected to frame the Regulations under the Act,  would now only be 
established once the new Act is passed and further the R ules/Regulations required 
under the Act would be delayed further. Committee is of the view that four years have ,

since, elapsed without any progress when so much importance is being given to Ease of 
Doing Business in Indi a which may adversely affect the confidence in the international 
business community who would like to invest in the country. The benefits would have 
been supposedly passed down to the common man or concerned persons if the ACI was 
established. The Committee observes with concern that the working system which is 
prevalent across the Departments/Ministry is not in accordance with the objective of the 
Governance. The Committee recommends that ACI should be established on priority. 
The Ministry needs to carry out necessary amendments in the Act to set it up keeping in 
view the upcoming general election next year. The Committee recommends that the 
pending actions may be completed by the month of December.

recommends that these timelines sought by the Ministries should be  adhered to be them 
at any cost.

observed that some Ministries have been seeking extension of time from the Committee 
a number of times, yet the framing of subordinate legis lation has not been completed. 
There is no limit to the number of extensions that can be sought by the Ministry. The 
Ministries have not adhered to the time limit granted to them by the Committee. The 
Committee’s role of monitoring whether subordinate legi slation have not been framed 
or the framing thereof has been inordinately delayed has been downplayed. In this 
regard, the Committee  suggested to have a discussion with the Hon’ble Chairman, 
Rajya Sabha along with the Secretaries of the concerned Ministri es so as to seek a 
solution through dialogue. Further as stated by the Ministries, extensions of time were 
sought from the Committee after taking due approval from the Hon’ble Ministers. 
Hence, in this reagrd, the Chairman of the Committee has written to t he concrened 
Hon’ble Ministers about the delay in framing of subordinate legislation under various 
acts pending in the Ministries.  
 

 
 
 
17 
 
44. The Committee observes that of late the requests for extension of time have 
almost become a routine and the Ministries have not been adhering to the time -limit of 
six months for framing subordinate legislation as earlier recommended by the 
Committee. The Committee has found that the Ministries have taken considerable time 
in framing of the rules/regulations and therefore t he Acts remain unimplemented or 
partially implemented. The Committee has, therefore, made very important 
recommendations/observations regarding the delay in framing of rules/regulations by 
the Ministries. In 1971 the Committee in its 9 th Report prescribed six months time limit 
for framing the subordinate legislation contemplated under the Act. However, in the 
same year the Committee in its 10th Report suggested that if Rules are not framed within 
the time limit of 6 months, the Secretary or Head of Departme nt should be informed

obtain his orders. The Committee proposes that the aforesaid observation of the 
Committee may be incorporated not only in new legislation and also in th e existing Acts

in framing of all necessary subordinate legislation contemplated under Acts of 
Parliament administered by various Ministries/Departments.

Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019  to institutionalize the arbitration 
proceedings wherein the Arbitration Council of India (ACI) was to be established.   With 
regard to the reasons for non-setting up the ACI till date, they informed the Committee that 
a number of stakeholders have  demanded autonomy for the ACI and that to enable

Government, the Bill for amended new Act providing for a revamped ACI in its

REPORT
I. Introduction and Background
1.1 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Bill, 2021 was introduced in Lok Sabha on July 30, 2021. This Bill provided for the constitution of a
Commission for better co-ordination, research, identification, and resolution of problems related to air
quality in the National Capital Region (NCR) and adjoining areas. Adjoining areas were defined as areas
in Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh, adjoining the National Capital Territory of Delhi and
NCR, where any source of pollution may cause adverse impact on air quality in the NCR. This Bill also
sought to dissolve the Environment Pollution Prevention and Control Authority established in the NCR in
1998. An Ordinance establishing a similar Commission was promulgated in October 2020 which lapsed
in March 2021 and was repromulgated in April 2021. This Bill repealed the 2021 Ordinance.
1.2 The Statement of Object and Reasons, with the Bill, succinctly stated that the Bill aimed to
establish a Commission for Air Quality Management in the National Capital Region (NCR) and its
adjoining areas to address the ongoing air pollution crisis while noting that despite efforts by Committees,
Courts, and ad hoc measures, air quality remains a significant concern in the region. Through the Bill, a
permanent, statutory authority with broad powers to tackle pollution, including controlling stubble
burning, vehicular emissions, industrial pollution, and other sources, through coordination between states
and various stakeholders was sought to be created. It was stated that the Bill will replace previous
temporary Committees and Ordinances, focusing on comprehensive, collaborative actions, and enforce
penalties for violations. The Bill also included sub-committees to support monitoring, enforcement, and
research efforts, ensuring long-term, effective solutions to air pollution.
1.3 The said Bill was passed by Houses of Parliament and notified on 13 thAugust, 2021 as“The
Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021”(CAQM Act
henceforth) (Annexure I) .
1.4 The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (Imposition,
Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023 and
subsequent amendments.
1.4.1 India is committed to create a clean environment and pollution free air as mandated in the
Constitution of India. The Committee appointed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 has taken
measures to deal with the menace of air pollution, particularly in the National Capital Region. By orders
1

passed from time to time, the courts have also set upad hoccommittees to aid and assist them on it
oringand implementation of its orders and generally to take steps to deal with air pollution. Even then,
quality of air in the air shed of the National Capital Region and in the adjoining areas remains a major
cause of concern. There is a need to evolve and implement a consolidated approach for monitoring,
tackling and eliminating the causes for air pollution and identifying, specifying and rigorously enforcing
measures for elimination and mitigation of air pollution, including but not limited to, controlling or
eliminating the activities of stubble burning, vehicular pollution, industrial emissions, road dust, biomass
burning and urban construction. To deal with the problem of Stubble Burning and fulfil the provision of
Section 15 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas Act,2021,The
Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and
Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023were framed and notified.
1.4.2 The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas(Imposition,
Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023 have been
framed in accordance with the provision in Section 15 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National CapitalRegion and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 which provides that “the Commission may
impose and collect environmental compensation from farmers causing air pollution by stubble burning, at
such rate and in such manner,as maybe prescribed”.
1.4.3Background of imposition of Environmental Compensation:Prior to the enactment of the
CAQM Act, the Hon’ble National Green Tribunal (Principal Bench),
New Delhi through its judgment dated 10.12.2015 in Application No. 118 of 2013 titled as 2.
Vikrant Kumar Tongad Vs. Environment Pollution (Prevention & Control) Authority & Ors.,inter alia,
directed as under:
“In view of the above discussion and the stand taken before us by the different State
Governments and the Ministry, we dispose of this application with the following directions:
XXX
All the States which have issued Notification prohibiting agriculture crop residue burning
shall ensure that the Notifications are enforced rigorously and proper action is taken against the
defaulters. Any person or body that is found offending this direction would be liable to pay
Environmental Compensation as follows:
a.Small land holders having an area less than 2 Acres shall pay Environmental Compensation
of Rs. 2500/- per incidence.
b.Land holders having land area more than 2 Acres but Less than 5 Acres shall pay
Environmental Compensation of Rs. 5000/- per incidence.
2

c.Land holders having land area more than 5 Acres shall pay Environmental Compensation of
Rs. 15000/-per incidence.”
State Governments had been imposing Environmental Compensation on the defaulters by following the
directions of Hon’ble Tribunal in the above-mentioned order.
1.4.4 Statutory Framework for imposition of Environmental Compensation:The Commission for
Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Ordinance, 2020 (No. 13 of
2020) was promulgated on 28.10.2020, for co-ordination, research, identification and resolution of
problems surrounding the air quality in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas. Upon it’s lapse, the
Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Ordinance,
2021 (No. 4 of 2021) was promulgated on 13.4.2021, for co-ordination, research, identification and
resolution of problems surrounding the air quality in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas.
Subsequently, The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining
Areas Act, 2021 (No. 29 of 2021) was enacted in the Parliament on 13.8.2021.
1.4.5 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Act, 2021 inter-alia has the following key provisions:
(a) Constitution of the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas to
perform the functions;
(b) Appointment of Chairperson, Members and Member-Secretary of the Commission
(c) Constitution of the Sub-committees on Monitoring and Identification, Safeguarding and
Enforcement, Research and Development;
(d) Powers and functions of the Commission to take all such measures and issue directions for the
purpose of protection and improvement of air quality in NCR and Adjoining Areas;
(e) Authorisation of any person by the Commission to perform the functions of the Commission;
(f) Commission to provide an effective framework, action plan and appropriate steps for tackling
the problem of stubble burning and monitor the measures taken by the States to prevent stubble
burning, in the NCR and Adjoining Areas;
(g) Penalty for contravention of provisions, rules, orders or directions issued by the Commission;
(h) Imposition and collection of Environmental Compensation from farmers causing air pollution
by stubble burning;
(i) Payment of grants by the Central Government to the Commission for its functioning;
(j) Maintaining accounts by the Commission and conducting audits;
3

(k) Powers of Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions.
1.4.6 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
(hereinafter referred to as the “Commission”) was constituted on 23.04.2021 in accordance with the
provisions of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining
Areas Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”). Section 14 of the Act provides for penalty for
contravention of provisions of the Act, rules, orders and directions issued by the Commission. Section 14
of the Act,inter alia,stipulates as under:
“(1) Any non-compliance or contravention of any provisions of this Act, rules made there under or any
order or direction issued by the Commission, shall be an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term
which may extend up to five years or with fine which may extend up to one crore rupees or with both:
Provided that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any farmer for causing air pollution
by stubble burning or mismanagement of agricultural residue.”
1.4.7 While Section 14(1) of the Act provides for punishment with imprisonment which may extend
upto five years or with fine which may extend upto one crore or with both for any non-compliance or
contraventions of the Act or rules or directions, the said provision is not applicable to any farmer for
causing air pollution by stubble burning or mismanagement of agricultural residue.
1.4.8 Accordingly, Section 15 of the Act, provides for imposition of Environmental Compensation on
farmers for causing air pollution by stubble burning. Section 15 of the Act,inter alia,stipulates as under:
“The Commission may impose and collect environmental compensation from farmers causing air
pollution by stubble burning, at such rate and in such manner, as may be prescribed.”
1.4.9 Section 25 provides for making rules by the Central Government to carry out the provisions of the
Act. Section 25 of the Act,inter-aliastipulates as under:
“(1) The Central Government may, by notification, make rules to carry out the provisions of this
Act.
(2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may
provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:—
xxxxx
(h) the rate at which, and the manner in which, the environmental compensation shall be
imposed and collected under section 15;”
1.4.10 In view of the provisions of the Act, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Changevideits Notification No. G.S.R. 322(E) dated 28.04.2023 notified the Commission for Air Quality
4

Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of
Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023,(Annexure II) which,inter alia,
stipulates as under:
“Imposition of environmental compensation for stubble burning.—The Commission may
impose and collect environmental compensation on farmers liable for burning stubble, at the
following rates, namely: -
(a) The Farmer having an area of land less than two acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of rupees two thousand five hundred;
(b) The Farmer having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres shall
pay an environmental compensation of rupees five thousand;
(c) The Farmers having an area of more than five acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of rupees fifteen thousand.”
1.4.11Amendment in the Extant Provision for implementation of Environmental Compensation:
The Hon’ble Supreme Court vide its Order dated 23.10.2024 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 13029 of 1985
in the matter of M.C. Mehta Vs. Union of India & Ors.,inter alia, observed and directed as under:
“…The environmental compensation that is stated to be recovered is minimal.
The learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the Commission states that the
Government of India has exercised power under Section 15 of the Commission for Air
Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 (for short, "the Act") and
has adopted the formula laid down by the National Green Tribunal for fixing rates of compensation while
framing Rules. Nothing is placed on record to show that the rulemaking power has been exercised in
terms of Section 15 of the Act prescribing the rates of compensation. The importance of Section 15 of the
Act has to be understood in the context of the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 14 of the Act, which
excludes the farmers from the applicability of penal provisions. When such a concession is given to the
farmers, power has to be exercised by the Government of India under Section 15 of the Act
by framing rules and by providing appropriate Environmental Compensation. The Government cannot
blindly rely upon the formula fixed by the National Green Tribunal.
We direct the Government of India to reconsider the issue and take action under Section
15 of the Act for prescribing proper rates of compensation. Section 15 of the Act talks about the
manner of collecting compensation. Unless proper exercise of power under Section 15 of the Act
is made, there cannot be any effective action against the wrongdoers. We expect the Government
to take actionwithin two weeks from today.”
1.4.12 The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, accordinglyvideNotification No.
G.S.R. 690(E) dated 06.11.2024, notified the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National
5

Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of Environmental
Compensation for Stubble Burning) Amendment Rules, 2024, (AnnexureIII)inter alia, substituting the
rule 3 as under:
“The Commission may impose environmental compensation as per the provisions of the Act
for stubble burning, at the following rates:-
(a) the Farmer having an area of land of less than two acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of five thousand rupees, per incidence;
(b) the Farmer having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres shall
pay an environmental compensation of ten thousand rupees, per incidence;
(c) the Farmer having an area of land of more than five acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of thirty thousand rupees, per incidence.”
Applicability of the CAQM Rules, 2023 is to the States of Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan
and NCT of Delhi.
1.5 Keeping in view its significance, the CAQM Rules 2023 was taken up for detailed examination
by the Committee. The Committee had sought information through Background notes and
Questionnaire from the nodal Ministry i.e. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for
their comments/clarifications. The subject was deliberated upon by the Committee in its two meetings
held on 3 rd and 18 th December, 2024. During the course of its examination, the Committee had long
ranging discussion with the representatives of the (i) Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate
Change, Commission for Air Quality Management and Central Pollution Control Board on 3 rd
December, 2024 and (ii) On 18 th December, 2024 with the representatives of the Ministries of
Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare, New and Renewable Energy, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Power,
Commerce and Industry (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal trade) besides the nodal
Ministry ( Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change). The Committee also heard experts on
the subject of stubble burning namely Dr. Suresh Jain, Professor of Air Pollution and Health,
Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology, Tirupati (Andhra
Pradesh) and Dr. Abhishek Kar, Senior Programme Lead, Council on Energy, Environment and Water,
Vasant Kunj Institutional area, New Delhi. .
1.6 In their submissions before the Committee the invited Ministries and the subject experts stated as
under:
1.6.1 Submissions by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry:Representatives from the Ministry of
Commerce and Industry presented their approach towards utilizing agricultural residues, particularly
parali, as an alternative fuel and raw material for various industries, including cement, paper, and
6

furniture manufacturing. The Ministry outlined a three-pronged strategy to explore these possibilities
through stakeholder consultations, research, and collaboration with national-level institutes. In their
submissions they highlighted that stubble, particularly rice straw, has significant potential in industries
such as construction, paper, and furniture manufacturing with key uses being identified as particle boards
for furniture and construction, pulp for paper production, including eco-friendly tableware and packaging-
